subject: Architecture
title: The Statue of Liberty: Engineering a Symbol
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Statue of Liberty: Engineering a Symbol.

hook.text: The Statue of Liberty's skin is thinner than two pennies stacked together.

buildup.text: Frédéric Bartholdi sculpted the copper exterior. Gustave Eiffel engineered the iron skeleton inside.

discovery.text: The statue was shipped from France in 350 pieces packed in 214 crates, then assembled on site.

twist.text: America couldn't afford the pedestal. Joseph Pulitzer raised funds through small newspaper donations.

climax.text: Its green color is natural patina — the original copper was shiny brown like a new penny.

punchline.text: France built it. America almost couldn't afford to stand it up.

quiz.question: Who engineered the Statue of Liberty's internal structure?

details.summary: The Statue of Liberty's copper skin is only 2.4 millimeters thick — supported by an iron skeleton designed by Gustave Eiffel. This curtain-wall approach separates the structural frame from the exterior surface.
details.whyItMatters: The Statue of Liberty pioneered the separation of structure and skin that later defined skyscraper construction. Eiffel's iron armature supporting a thin copper curtain wall anticipated the curtain-wall technology that transformed 20th-century.
takeaways: Copper skin is only 2.4mm thick on an iron armature by Gustave Eiffel
The curtain-wall approach separates structure from exterior surface
This anticipated modern skyscraper curtain-wall construction

faq.question: Why is the Statue of Liberty green?
faq.answer: The original copper skin was a shiny penny color when installed in 1886. Over about 20 years, exposure to air and rain caused a chemical reaction (patina) that turned the copper green. The patina actually protects the underlying copper from further corrosion, acting as a natural preservative.

faq.question: What structural problems has the statue faced?
faq.answer: Galvanic corrosion between the iron armature and copper skin was a major issue. When dissimilar metals touch in the presence of moisture, they corrode. A 1980s restoration replaced the iron armature with stainless steel and added Teflon barriers between the metals to prevent future corrosion.
